paragraphs: The wind of Hexi had a cutting edge.

On entering the corridor, fine sand worked its way down men’s collars and stung their eyes. Farther west, even the sand thinned; the country lay bare in gravel and yellow-white ribs of mountain. Liang Hu worked his spade half a day before cutting a trench barely a foot deep outside his tent, and broke two handles doing it. Zhao An crouched by the hole, felt the hardened earth beneath, and told someone to pour a dipper of water onto it.

Manu clutched the waterskin and refused. Liang Hu called him stingy; Manu cursed back in Qiang. Qifu Wu understood and laughed so hard he fell over. A local Liangzhou guide passing by told them that any water poured into this ground would leave a crust of salt after dark. All of them turned toward Zhao An. He slid his knife into its sheath and cleared his throat. “Then we camp somewhere else.”
Moving a tent was easier than arguing. But five days later they found that their next water source lay beneath the arrows of a Liang outpost.

Murong Chui refused his commanders' requests to storm the fort. He sent light Xianbei cavalry to cut two relay roads, while Han infantry escorted water carts through a southern pass and around the rear of the position. Qiang archers lay all night along a ridge without loosing a single arrow. At daybreak the defenders found both roads barred. They drove their last forty-odd horses north and fled, abandoning dozens of hungry wounded and a well long since dry.
“Do we give them water?” a Xianbei lieutenant asked.
“Yes,” said Murong Chui.
“Our own men are short.”
“Then reduce the general’s tent allowance first.”

That same day a small Liangzhou detachment surrendered its arms. Qin clerks were preparing to count armor, then prisoners, when they discovered that more than ten Qin civilians had been marched among the captives. One still had raw rope wounds on his wrists and ankles. He held an empty cloth sack so tightly that no one could prise it from his hands. Liang Hu offered him half his own bag of roasted millet. The man stared at it and asked, suddenly, “Are you truly Qin soldiers?”
“The banner’s outside,” Liang Hu answered.
“The men who took us said they were government troops too.”
Liang Hu opened his mouth, but no reply came. The man tipped the millet into his sack and still would not eat.

The Qin army moved west along the old merchant road, thirty thousand men with different work to do. A few thousand cavalry in front cut raiders off from their retreat. The main force controlled three passes. Grain escorts and road crews traveled back and forth for hundreds of miles. Murong Chui’s banner was always the most visible thing on the highway, but few ever saw thirty thousand men gathered beneath it ready to charge. Newly arrived officers could not understand why generals in former days had taken cities at the first chance, while these men seized a water source and then sat guarding it for ten days.
A dispute over rations and merit reached the command tent faster than any enemy army.

A Xianbei squad leader presented the names of seven captives and demanded credit for seven kills. The records officer studied the depositions and allowed credit for two soldiers; the other five had been merchants driven along the road under guard. The squad leader slammed the register so hard it jumped on the table. In the next tent a Han captain was furious that his men had repaired two bridges and escorted seven hundred grain wagons, yet received only the words “diligent service” in the merit book. The Qiang archers were angrier still. After three days at the outposts, their dried meat had been reassigned to the cavalry, and now they faced the supply guards with bows strung.

Murong Chui came to the grain scales and first ordered every bow unstrung. He then had the units report their marches and sick lists for the past three days. Sweat ran down the quartermaster’s forehead as he explained that cavalry were traditionally issued more meat and beans to keep up their strength.
“Which cavalry?” Murong Chui asked. “The horses eat beans; the riders eat beans. What do the archers who walked sixty li on the western slope eat?”

No one answered. Murong Chui made the quartermaster straighten the scales with his own hands and adjust the next three days' portions according to actual consumption. The works officers and army physicians were told to report mileage, duty hours, injuries, and illness together. He did not discover a rule that would serve for all time. Three days later men still argued beside the scales, but they brought march records and sick lists instead of merely pounding their chests and claiming to have suffered most.

A young Han clerk, angry enough to lose sleep, wrote two characters meaning “service merit” in the margin of the campaign register. Under them he entered bridge repair, guard duty, grain escort, and rescue of the wounded, one by one. There was no provision in the old rewards system for any of it, so he left blank spaces for a superior’s later judgment. When Murong Chui noticed the addition next morning, he asked who had authorized it. The young man’s face went white, but he said softly, “Without that column, the four men who died on the bridge yesterday have no names anywhere except the casualty roll.”
Murong Chui leafed through the book. “Keep it,” he said. “But promise no rewards before the claims are verified.”

The clerk sat down in astonishment, having expected a beating. That afternoon several works officers arrived, demanding credit for a bridge their men had failed to complete. Only then did he understand that the trouble he had started by writing two characters was just beginning.

By late summer more and more Qin captives had been recovered, though hundreds remained missing. Many of the abducted children could not remember their native districts. Some knew only that their mothers had called them Shi’er. Others could sing a song from home but could not name the river beside their villages. The army clerks refused to enter “without registration” against their names. On separate sheets they began a family-search register, recording a red birthmark behind an ear, the color of an old coat, the age at which each child had been taken. Manu saw a boy with half his little finger missing. He spread his own hand and asked if a horse rein had severed it. The boy shook his head and murmured, “Last winter.” No one asked him anything else.
It was then that Suo Gong came from Former Liang.

A former official of Jincheng Commandery, he wore a faded blue robe and traveled with two attendants bearing official credentials. There was not a valuable ornament about him. When he met Murong Chui, he first asked for the return of the intercepted Liang soldiers, then offered a peace proposal jointly signed by several border garrisons.
“Where is Zhang Tianxi’s seal?” Murong Chui asked.
“In Guzang, whoever affixes a seal now earns the hatred of the other faction.”
“Have you come to make peace or to lay your difficulties at the Qin camp?”
“Only to reopen the trade road. People in Jincheng dared hardly travel last year. This year even salt is being fought over by the measure.”
“Return the Qin civilians you took first.”
“We will do our utmost within three days.”
“Your utmost is not enough.”
Suo Gong looked down at the family-search register on the table. “General, what if some have already died along the way?”
Murong Chui raised his eyes. “Then tell their families where they are buried.”
Suo Gong’s lips moved without sound. For months he had heard Qin soldiers threaten to destroy Liang. No one had asked about the dead in that way.

Three days later Suo Gong delivered more than six hundred people. Others were still unaccounted for. Some had fled, some had died of illness, and some had been sold on. Murong Chui forbade the case to be marked “transfer completed.” He had every missing person entered in a second document and sent it back with the envoy to Guzang for further inquiry.

The Qin army was still more than a hundred li east of Guzang when Fu Jian’s second edict reached Murong Chui from Chang’an. It authorized him to escort the returned captives, establish protective camps around Guzang, and pursue negotiations. If inhabitants voluntarily sought shelter, the Qin troops could temporarily take charge of the gates, granaries, and offices to meet an emergency. A mounted courier must report to the court at once; the army could not settle the fall of a state or its future allegiance on its own authority. Even if Former Liang refused to return the remaining captives, the army was not to storm Guzang in anger.
“Does His Majesty want us to fight or not?” a Xianbei officer muttered after hearing it.

Murong Chui folded the edict. “He wants us to spare him the dead an assault would bring. If you can keep the people of a city alive by reading out an edict, you can save me the trouble of commanding.”

The Qin camp edged closer to Guzang. Protective posts interrupted traffic on three sides; the northern road remained open to civilians. Merchants traveling between Liangzhou and the outside had to pass inspections by both armies and often lost days on a single journey. Within the city, suspicion spread. Zhang Tianxi’s intimates called for resistance, merchants wanted the roads reopened, and border officials wanted someone—anyone—to feed the starving. Great families kept their private granaries locked while the government stores ran dry. When Suo Gong returned to the city, he was confined in a side courtyard of his own home and forbidden visitors.
Yet the most impatient men of all were in the Qin camp.

Fu Yi, an officer of the imperial Fu clan, commanded eight hundred men. Since youth he had fought beside veteran Guanzhong troops and was famous for leading desperate charges. Now every reckoning of merit set road crews and granary guards alongside him, brandishing papers and demanding credit. His resentment had grown. Someone reported that a defender of the north gate would open it for Qin troops, giving as proof a broken green-lacquered crossbow bolt. No scout or relay station had confirmed the message. Fu Yi nevertheless hid the bolt in his sleeve and summoned his officers after dark.
“Headquarters has issued a secret order. The north gate can be taken,” he said.
A Han squad leader was doubtful. “If the general has received a secret order, does he have the commander’s token?”
Fu Yi looked at him coldly. “The emperor’s name is Fu. Must I borrow a surname from you before I act?”

The squad leader fell silent. A few older men noticed that something was wrong: the token lacked a countersign, and the messenger was not one they knew from headquarters. One slipped away behind the camp to report it. By then Fu Yi had armed his troops and marched out.

The moon that night was thin as a silver needle. The drawbridge at the north gate lowered halfway. There really were lamps flickering inside the gate. The vanguard crossed, the rear ranks following close. Just as the three-hundredth man entered the outer barbican, the inner gate slammed shut and the outer bridge rose sharply on its ropes. Torches blazed all at once along the walls. Logs and stones crashed down on either side; shouts, screaming horses, and shattering armor filled the narrow passage, until no sound could be distinguished from any other.

Liang Hu’s squad had been on duty at the southern camp. By the time they reached the north gate, wounded men were already piled beneath it. Someone raised a ladder to reach the soldiers trapped in the barbican and took an arrow through the body as soon as he looked up. Liang Hu was about to rush forward when Zhao An seized the straps of his armor.
“How do you expect to get up there?”
“Our men are inside!”
“And if you go, they’ll have one more corpse to carry out!”

They were almost grappling with each other when a mounted messenger from Murong Chui arrived. The outer units were to form a shield line and cover any retreating men; no detachment was to attack another gate without orders. Archers advanced behind the shields along a drainage ditch and dragged back wounded men one group after another. None of them could reach those inside the barbican. Before dawn, the cries from the walls dwindled away.

At the reckoning, more than three hundred and seventy Qin soldiers were dead, over two hundred wounded, and another hundred or so taken prisoner. Names filled the casualty register line after line. When the paper ran out, clerks wrote on the backs of old grain accounts. Two men’s faces had been destroyed by arrows; only the military tags at their waists identified them. Another man’s tag was half burned away, and fellow soldiers argued over two different names until they dared not even say with certainty where the dead man had come from.
Murong Chui examined the tags and the forged command token in his headquarters, then ordered Fu Yi brought in.
Fu Yi had been struck in the left arm. Blood showed through his white bandage. He saluted the seated commander with folded hands but refused to kneel.
“My night attack failed. I will answer for the defeat.”
“Who gave the order?”
“I acted on the opportunity before me.”
“You told eight hundred men I had given you a secret command.”
Fu Yi compressed his lips. “Had the general attacked earlier, that gate would never have stood open for nothing.”

Murong Chui had the military judge lay three depositions, the false token, and the movement register on the table. He did not pronounce sentence at once. He made Fu Yi read the Han squad leader’s statement and had the scouts identify the forged token in person. Only then did he ask, “Those men wagered their lives on your claim of a secret order. Will you make them bear its burden as well?”
Fu Yi stared at the token and suddenly shouted, “Even if I moved troops without permission, I must be tried by the Imperial Clan Court! What right has a man of Yan to kill a man of the Fu house?”

Word of it spread through the camp. Several veteran Di officers knelt and pleaded for him, saying that Fu Yi had won many battles and that a clansman’s offense should be referred to Chang’an. The Xianbei officers, by contrast, hardly dared speak. They knew that if Murong Chui executed Fu Yi, the old Yan faction would gain nothing; the whole new army might be the loser.

That night the military judge returned with the relevant articles. The code prescribed execution at the front for forging a commander’s orders and starting unauthorized hostilities resulting in deaths. It made no exemption for imperial kinsmen, but required the military judge and two supervising officers to sign the verdict together. The two supervisors argued for hours. One feared punishment by association and would not put his name to the paper. The other wanted the depositions carried at full speed to Chang’an for a final decision. Murong Chui listened without insulting them. He asked only, “If we wait for a reply and someone else brings a forged token to move the cavalry, which order will you obey first?”

By daybreak all three examiners had signed. As their seals came down on the paper, Fu Yi was straightening his robes with his uninjured hand. Before the execution he requested one last audience with Murong Chui.
“General,” he asked, “if I had succeeded last night, would you still kill me today?”
Murong Chui pushed the bamboo slips of military law toward him. “Read it yourself.”
Fu Yi did not read. After looking at him for a long time, he laughed. “Do you imagine the Fu family will not hate you for this?”
“They will.”
“Even His Majesty may not protect you.”
“I know.”
Fu Yi studied him. For a moment a strange trace of respect came into his eyes, then vanished. “Then get on with it.”

No one cheered beneath the execution platform at noon. Just before the blade fell, Fu Yi struggled to look toward the north gate. His gaze still sought the drawbridge of the night before. Blood ran between the boards. Several old soldiers turned their faces away. Murong Chui ordered the execution record, the investigation papers, and the casualty rolls sealed and sent to Chang’an. Fu Yi’s former military merits were not to be erased; his family was not to be punished with him; the soldiers who had followed the forged order would be judged according to what each had actually done.
A Di lieutenant wept. “Now you’ve beheaded him, the imperial clan in Guanzhong will demand your life.”
Murong Chui looked toward Guzang’s distant walls. Only after a long silence did he answer, “Then live long enough to return and tell them exactly what you saw today.”

When Fu Rong reached the forward camp, the platform had been washed, though dark-red stains remained between the boards. He read the three sealed records without raising his head. “How am I to explain this to my brother in Chang’an?”

Murong Chui sat opposite him. “If the edict lets a commander enforce military law in the field, but he draws back whenever a clansman stands before him, whose orders will thirty thousand men obey tomorrow?”

“You have your reasons,” Fu Rong said slowly. “But part of the blame for those three hundred and seventy deaths is yours as well. You brought the siege to the city and let impatience grow among the troops.”

Murong Chui was silent for a long time. Then he put a broken military tag in Fu Rong’s hand. It belonged to an unidentified soldier dragged from the barbican. The back of the wooden tag was charred black.
“That blame is mine.”

The report stirred Chang’an as expected. The imperial clan demanded punishment for Murong Chui’s unauthorized execution of a kinsman. Fu Pi slapped his court tablet against his palm in anger. Yao Chang asked only whether the military judge’s three seals were all present. The ministers accused him of making light of the matter. He bowed his head, acknowledged their rebuke, and said nothing more. Fu Jian summoned the military code promulgated after the surrender of the tallies in the eleventh year of Jianyuan. He read the depositions alongside Fu Yi’s record of service. Two palace lamps burned down before dawn, when at last he wrote at the foot of the dispatch: The sentence has been carried out. The commander shall not be prosecuted for it. The casualties and the origin of the false order must be investigated further. Command responsibility remains; one execution cannot answer for all the dead.
By the time the reply reached Hexi, autumn had begun to cool the wind.

The people of Guzang first heard that the Qin army had executed a member of the imperial clan, then that it had not attacked the city in retaliation. The hardliners had held the north gate, waiting each day for the Qin troops to storm it in anger, so that the whole city would at last commit itself to resistance. Instead, the Qin army posted the names of prisoners outside the walls and proposed exchanges. It published hours when civilians might leave to draw water, along with the prices of grain. Private granaries remained locked. Bodies of those who had starved began to be carried from the lanes. Suo Gong was released from confinement. Several officials sought him out and asked, “Can the Qin proclamations be trusted?”
Suo Gong answered, “An order is a piece of paper. To know if it can be trusted, we must see how they treat the people we send out today.”
“And if they break their promises once we open the gates?”
“Then I will die before you do.”

After nightfall the lamps at the east gate went out three times. Murong Chui remembered the drawbridge at the north gate. When the message reached him he did not move the army. He first sent ten envoys carrying white lamps and wearing no heavy armor. When the gate opened, Suo Gong and several Liangzhou officials were indeed waiting behind it. Guards lined both sides, weapons raised, every palm slick with sweat.
“Where is Zhang Tianxi?” Murong Chui called across the threshold.
“Still in the palace. Some wish to escort him west; others would persuade him to hear peace terms.”
“The north gate?”
“There are men still resolved to defend it.”
“The granaries?”
Suo Gong hesitated. “The public stores remain. The private owners refuse to open theirs.”

Murong Chui gave his orders. One unit was to receive the gate, another guard the granaries, and a third patrol outside the residential wards. No detachment was to enter a private home without orders from headquarters. Suo Gong signed a document authorizing temporary military custody of the defenses. The Qin supervisor countersigned it, and a swift rider left for Chang’an to request a ruling on Liangzhou’s allegiance. The old Liang banners remained in the city; the Qin army did not order them struck down at once. The gate had been opened to save a city from starvation. Who would govern it was a matter for the imperial decree and for the work that lay ahead inside the walls.

When the east gate opened, no townspeople lined the street to welcome the newcomers. Doors opened only in narrow cracks, showing a child’s eyes, a woman’s hand, or a short knife hidden beneath a sleeve. Liang Hu’s squad was assigned to guard a granary. Qifu Wu caught sight of a fat sheep tethered outside a house and could not stop looking. Liang Hu prodded him with his scabbard. “Keep your eyes where they belong.”

Manu picked up a toy windmill crushed beneath passing feet and laid it gently on a doorstep. A little boy came forward to retrieve it, but his mother seized him and pulled him back inside. Manu waited a while, then returned to his squad. Even when his watch ended, the broken toy still lay beyond the threshold.

The north-city defenders refused to surrender their weapons. At dawn an old Liang banner suddenly rose above the wall. An officer shouted down that Liangzhou would never submit to Qin and cut his own throat. Some followers threw themselves from the battlements; others turned their blades upon themselves. One man tried to join them but could not force his hand to his neck and collapsed weeping. More than seventy lay dead together. Blood quickly filled the seams between the stones. The Qin army had not stormed the wall, and no one cheered.

When Murong Chui climbed the wall, he found a young defender still faintly breathing, a self-inflicted blade wound in his belly. The army physician tried to help him, but the youth struggled and cursed. “Don’t touch me.”
“What is your name?” Murong Chui asked.
“Liu Duan.”
“From Guzang?”
“The southern ward. My mother... she’s in the southern ward.”
“Find his mother and bring her here.”
Liu Duan opened unfocused eyes. Seeing the Qin cloak about Murong Chui’s shoulders, he suddenly asked, “Are you the Prince of Wu who served Yan?”
Murong Chui nodded.
“Your country is gone too. How do you bear being alive?”
For a long while Murong Chui said nothing. The physician pressed a hand to the wound. Liu Duan bit his sleeve against the pain; blood seeped from the corner of his mouth.
“I am alive,” Murong Chui said at last.
The boy gave a cold little laugh, as though he meant to mock him, but had no strength. When the physician carried him down from the wall, he still gripped a short sword with no scabbard.
Suo Gong stood among the bodies, his voice raw. “General, you came too late.”

Murong Chui neither defended himself nor argued that an earlier assault would have killed more. He watched the Qin soldiers pitching camp outside the walls and remembered the line of wooden tags left by Fu Yi’s night attack. Inside the city and beyond it, everyone could claim a great cause for which men had died. At the doors of their homes, it was always a mother, a child, a face from which even the name had been lost.

In the end, several close attendants escorted Zhang Tianxi to the Qin camp. What they brought was a petition of surrender, not a list of men to execute. Murong Chui sealed it and reported the facts to Chang’an, awaiting orders. He could temporarily secure the defenses and forbid harm to civilians, but had no authority to decide the fate of the Former Liang royal house on the spot. When officers grumbled that they had marched all the way to a capital without even a formal ceremony of captive presentation, he asked, “Whose head did you intend to bring back for your reward?” No one answered.

Outside the city seventy-three new mounds formed a common grave for the northern defenders. Before Chang’an’s reply arrived, a washed old Liang banner had been set before them. Some objected that raising the flag of a lost state was inauspicious; others feared that seeing it would unsettle the Qin soldiers. Murong Chui ordered the dead buried according to their own military rites. Former Liang clerks were to verify each name. Spaces would be left for the unknown until their families came to claim them.
A young Qin soldier asked, “General, they would sooner die than surrender. Why go to all this trouble?”
“If you died in Hexi, you too would want someone to send your name home to Chang’an.”
Then he walked alone among the new graves. Wind came through a pass of the Qilian Mountains and pressed the paper mourning banners flat against the yellow earth. They could not rise.

Guzang’s east gate stood open again. Merchants ventured in and out with their carts; children at last dared put a foot beyond the cracks in their doors. The courier from Chang’an was still on the road. The city’s old plaques still hung in place, and beside them the Qin soldiers had posted only a temporary order securing its defenses.

Murong Chui remembered the first time he had walked outside the palace walls at Ye. The hatred he carried then had burned more fiercely than anything he had seen in Liu Duan’s eyes today. He too had believed that once a kingdom fell, there could be no life afterward.
Now he stood on the other side of the walls, still not knowing how to grant a person who had lost his country the peace of sleep.
